title: Piperacillin-Tazobactam
sources: Roberts JA, et al. DALI study — defining antibiotic levels in intensive care unit patients. Clin Infect Dis. 2014;58(8):1072-1083 (PK/PD rationale for extended infusion in critical illness).
Lodise TP Jr, et al. Piperacillin-tazobactam for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection: clinical implications of an extended-infusion dosing strategy. Clin Infect Dis. 2007;44(3):357-363.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap; vancomycin was the only antimicrobial dosing card until this batch. Standard extended-infusion regimen given with confidence; renal-adjustment presented qualitatively rather than as a precise numeric table, since critically ill patients frequently have AUGMENTED (not reduced) renal clearance and institutional CrCl-tiered protocols vary — a false-precision table risks being wrong in the direction that matters (under-dosing a septic patient with a normal or high CrCl).

mechanism: Broad-spectrum beta-lactam (piperacillin) plus a beta-lactamase inhibitor (tazobactam) — covers most gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, gram-positives, and anaerobes. Bactericidal effect is time-dependent (time above MIC), which is why infusion duration matters as much as the dose itself.
onset: Within the first infusion, but time-to-therapeutic-exposure depends heavily on infusion strategy (see dosing).
duration: Redosed every 6-8 h depending on renal function and infusion strategy.
dosing:
Standard (normal renal function): 4.5 g IV q6h or q8h.
Extended-infusion strategy (preferred in critical illness/sepsis): the SAME 4.5 g dose infused over 4 hours rather than the traditional 30 minutes — this keeps free drug concentrations above the MIC for a much larger fraction of the dosing interval, which is what actually drives bacterial killing for this class. Increasingly the standard approach in ICU sepsis protocols, not just a specialist option.
Renal impairment: reduce the dose and/or extend the interval as CrCl falls — but critically ill patients frequently have AUGMENTED renal clearance (CrCl > 130 mL/min is common in young, hyperdynamic sepsis patients), which can under-dose a STANDARD regimen, not just a reduced one. Use your institution's renal/ARC dosing protocol or pharmacy consult for anything outside straightforward normal renal function — precise CrCl-tiered numbers vary enough by source and patient population that a single fixed table here would risk more harm than help.
cautions: AEs: interstitial nephritis (usually reversible), rash, GI upset, and rare but described neurotoxicity (seizures) at very high exposure, especially in renal impairment.
Precautions: contains a significant sodium load per gram — consider in heart failure/fluid-restricted patients on repeated high-dose therapy.
Precautions: does NOT reliably cover MRSA, atypicals, or most fungi — pair with the appropriate agent per your empiric-antibiotic pathway when those are on the differential.
pearls: The extended-infusion strategy uses the identical total daily dose as standard dosing — it's a delivery-method change, not a bigger dose, so it doesn't need a separate 'extended-infusion dose' number.

A falsely elevated PT/aPTT and even bleeding have been reported with high-dose piperacillin-tazobactam via platelet dysfunction — worth remembering in a patient on it who develops unexplained bleeding or coagulation-panel derangement.
